5th-dalai-lama: He was born in late 1617 as Künga Migyur in the Chonggye Valley in Ü, about two days' journey south-east of Lhasa, into the aristocratic Zahor family, whose seat since the 14th century was Taktsé Castle. His father, Dudul Rabten, was arrested in 1618 for taking part in a plot against Karma Phuntsok Namgyal, leader of the Tsang hegemony. The child's name was drawn by lot from three candidates in divination rituals held in secret at Radeng monastery, because the king of Tsang had forbidden the search for the 4th Dalai Lama's reincarnation. Sonam Choephel, the 4th Dalai Lama's chief attendant, is credited with finding him.

He received the name Lobsang Gyatso when he took novice ordination at Drepung, and Ngawang was added at his full ordination at the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa in 1638. Though a Gelug scholar, he also studied Nyingma doctrines and took Nyingma tantric empowerments.

Sonam Choephel, regent in his youth, asked Güshi Khan, head of the Khoshut, to act militarily in the Dalai Lama's name. Güshi Khan conquered Kham in 1640, and his victory over Karma Tenkyong, prince of Tsang, at Shigatse in 1642 completed the conquest and established the Khoshut Khanate. The Dalai Lama was then invested with temporal power over Tibet. He again proclaimed Lhasa the capital, as Songtsen Gampo had, appointed governors and ministers, promulgated laws, and made his regent a prime minister, the Desi.

He began building the Potala Palace in 1645 on a site between Drepung and Sera monasteries, and moved into the White Palace in 1649; the Red Palace was added in 1690–1694. He was the first Dalai Lama to accept an invitation from a Chinese emperor to visit Beijing. At his request the Panchen Lama Lobsang Chökyi Gyaltsen, his tutor, accepted Tashilhunpo Monastery as his seat for future incarnations. In 1679 he launched an expedition against his Prime Minister's advice, leading to the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War, which ended in 1684 with the Treaty of Tingmosgang.

He died in 1682 at the age of 65. His death was concealed by his Prime Minister, Desi Sangye Gyatso, so that the Potala could be finished and to prevent Tibet's neighbours from exploiting a gap in the succession. He wrote 24 volumes of scholarly and religious works, among them a detailed history of Tibet written in 1643 at Güshi Khan's request. Tibetans call him the Great Fifth.
